title: Selling a Vehicle With a Bonded Title
excerpt: You can sell it, and you do not have to wait for the bond term to end. What changes is what you should tell the buyer.
metaDescription: Selling a car with a bonded title: whether you can, what transfers to the buyer, how it affects price, and what to disclose.

body.text: You can sell a vehicle with a bonded title, and you do not need to wait for the bond term to end. The title transfers like any other. What changes is the conversation with the buyer, and handling that badly costs more than the notation itself does.

The buyer gets a title carrying the bonded notation for whatever remains of the term. If you bought the bond two years into a three-year term, they carry one year. When that year is up the notation stops applying for them exactly as it would have for you.

The bond stays in your name. You bought it, it guarantees your claim of ownership, and selling the vehicle does not transfer that obligation. If a valid claim is made during the term, the surety pays the claimant and looks to you, not to the person who bought the car.
What it does to your price

Less than most sellers fear, and more than it should, because buyers routinely confuse a bonded title with a salvage brand. The two are unrelated, as [bonded title vs. salvage and rebuilt titles](/bonded-title-vs-salvage-and-rebuilt-titles) sets out, and a buyer who understands the difference will not discount much.

A buyer checking the [national title record](https://vehiclehistory.bja.ojp.gov/) will see the vehicle's brand history, which is exactly the check you want them to make, because it shows the vehicle is not branded.

items: That the title is bonded, and when the term ends.
Why it was bonded: a lost title and a title that was never delivered are different stories, and the honest one is usually reassuring.
That the bond remains in your name and does not become their obligation.
Anything your state requires in writing on the bill of sale.

body.text: Volunteering this is the right call commercially as well as ethically. A buyer who discovers the notation at the counter walks away; a buyer told upfront usually does not. It also helps to be able to explain [how title bonds protect buyers](/how-title-bonds-protect-buyers-from-fraudulent-vehicle-titles) rather than leaving them to guess.

Waiting for the term to end leaves you with an ordinary title and no conversation to have. Whether that is worth it depends on how much of the term is left, which [what happens when your bonded title expires](/what-happens-when-your-bonded-title-expires) can help you judge.
